config.title: Unnecessary Re-renders

intro.title: Unnecessary Re-renders
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular counter application to understand and fix unnecessary re-renders. You will learn how Angular's change detection can cause components to re-render even when their data hasn't changed, which can hurt performance. The core concept involves using Angular's OnPush change detection strategy and pure pipes to control when updates occur. You'll work with components, templates, and lifecycle hooks to optimize your app.
intro.usecase: Unnecessary re-renders are a critical performance concern in real-world Angular applications, especially in data-intensive interfaces like financial dashboards or e-commerce product filters. For example, updating a single stock price in a live dashboard shouldn't cause the entire chart and table to re-render, as this would degrade the user experience with lag and high CPU usage. Similarly, in a large form with dependent fields, changing one input should not trigger re-evaluation of every other field's validation logic. By mastering techniques to prevent these wasteful updates, developers ensure their applications remain responsive and scalable under real user loads.

objectives: Identify components that trigger unnecessary re-renders in an Angular application
Apply the OnPush change detection strategy to optimize component rendering
Construct immutable data patterns to prevent unintended re-renders
Configure input property tracking to control when components update
Implement pure pipes to transform data without causing re-renders
Manipulate component lifecycle hooks to optimize change detection
Bind event handlers efficiently to minimize template re-evaluations

steps.title: Import Angular core modules and Component decorator
steps.instruction: Import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common' to set up the foundation for your Angular component.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with the correct module paths. Both imports should be on separate lines.
steps.seedCode: // Import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary Angular core modules are imported, enabling component creation and common directives.
successCriteria: Component is imported from '@angular/core' and CommonModule is imported from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've imported both Component and CommonModule with the correct syntax and paths.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Remember to import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.

steps.title: Create the main component class with @Component decorator
steps.instruction: Create a class named AppComponent and decorate it with @Component, setting selector to 'app-root' and template to an empty string initially.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator above the class definition. The selector should be a string 'app-root' and template an empty string ''.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent class is defined with the @Component decorator configured as specified.
successCriteria: AppComponent class exists, is decorated with @Component, has selector 'app-root' and template ''.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the class is named AppComponent, uses the @Component decorator with selector 'app-root' and template ''.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class isn't set up correctly. Check that you have the @Component decorator with the right configuration.

steps.title: Initialize component state with primitive values
steps.instruction: Inside the AppComponent class, add three properties: count as a number initialized to 0, name as a string initialized to 'Angular', and isActive as a boolean initialized to true.
steps.hint: Define these properties directly in the class body, using TypeScript type annotations and initial values.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have three typed properties with initial values that can be used in the template.
successCriteria: AppComponent has count: number = 0, name: string = 'Angular', and isActive: boolean = true defined as properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some properties, but make sure all three are present with correct types and initial values: count (number=0), name (string='Angular'), isActive (boolean=true).
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class doesn't have the required properties. Add count, name, and isActive with their specified types and initial values inside the AppComponent class.

steps.title: Create a method to update the count state
steps.instruction: Inside the AppComponent class, add a method named incrementCount that increments the count property by 1.
steps.hint: Define a method with no parameters that uses this.count to access and modify the count property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a method that can be called to update the count state, demonstrating how state changes trigger re-renders.
successCriteria: The AppComponent class contains a method named incrementCount that increments the count property by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a method, but check that it's named incrementCount and correctly increments the count property by 1 using this.count.
steps.feedbackWrong: The incrementCount method is missing or doesn't correctly update the count property. Make sure to add a method that increments this.count by 1.

steps.title: Create a method to update the name state
steps.instruction: In the AppComponent class, add a method named updateName that changes the name property to 'Updated Angular'.
steps.hint: Define a method inside the class with the updateName name. Inside the method, assign the new value to this.name.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a method that updates the name state, demonstrating how different state updates can trigger re-renders.
successCriteria: The AppComponent class contains an updateName method that sets this.name to 'Updated Angular'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a method, but it might not be named correctly or might not update the name property to 'Updated Angular'. Check the method name and assignment.
steps.feedbackWrong: The updateName method is missing or doesn't correctly update the name property. Make sure to add a method named updateName that sets this.name = 'Updated Angular'.

steps.title: Add basic template structure with interpolation
steps.instruction: Update the component's template property to display the count, name, and isActive values using Angular interpolation syntax: {{count}}, {{name}}, and {{isActive}}.
steps.hint: In the @Component decorator, replace the empty template string with a template that shows the three state values. Use double curly braces for interpolation.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component template will show the current values of count, name, and isActive using interpolation, demonstrating basic data binding.
successCriteria: The template property contains interpolation expressions for count, name, and isActive.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct interpolation syntax {{ }} for all three values: count, name, and isActive.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't yet show the state values. Remember to use double curly braces {{ }} around the property names.

steps.title: Add buttons to trigger state updates
steps.instruction: Add two buttons to the template: one with a click event bound to incrementCount() labeled 'Increment Count', and another with a click event bound to updateName() labeled 'Update Name'.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax (eventName)="handler()" for the click events. Place the buttons inside the existing template.
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will have two buttons that trigger the incrementCount and updateName methods when clicked.
successCriteria: Two buttons are present in the template with correct (click) event bindings to incrementCount() and updateName(), and appropriate labels.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that both buttons have the correct (click) event bindings and labels.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are missing or have incorrect event bindings. Make sure to use Angular's (click) syntax and bind to the correct methods.

steps.title: Add a console log to demonstrate re-renders
steps.instruction: Inside the AppComponent constructor, add a console.log() statement that logs 'Component rendered' to the console.
steps.hint: The constructor is a special method that runs when the component is first created. Add your console.log() statement inside the constructor body.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will log 'Component rendered' to the browser console when it first loads.
successCriteria: The AppComponent constructor contains a console.log() statement that logs 'Component rendered'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the console.log() statement is inside the constructor and logs exactly 'Component rendered'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The console.log() statement should be inside the AppComponent constructor and log 'Component rendered'.

steps.title: Test the application and observe re-renders
steps.instruction: Run the application in your development environment,
steps.hint: Make sure your development server is running. Open the browser's developer tools console to see the log messages when you interact with the buttons.
steps.expectedOutcome: When you click either button, the console will log 'Component rendered' each time, demonstrating that any state change triggers a complete component re-render.
successCriteria: Application runs successfully, clicking either button logs 'Component rendered' to the console, and you can observe that both state changes trigger re-renders.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're observing the console output when clicking both buttons. Each click should log 'Component rendered' regardless of which state changed.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: 1) Ensure your development server is running, 2) Open browser developer tools console, 3) Click both buttons and check if 'Component rendered' appears in the console each time.
